case_studies.title: InferD: A Honeypot Framework for AI Inference Infrastructure
case_studies.abstract: Large language model serving stacks, commercial inference APIs, vector databases, and agent orchestration gateways are now ex- posed on the public internet and indexed by commodity scanners within hours of deployment. The threat characteristics of this sur- face are only beginning to be measured, and the honeypot frame- works that could measure it were designed for conventional net- work services rather than for AI infrastructure. In fact, emulating an AI service is a distinct deception problem: the observable behavior of the service, including model inventories, token formats, tool-call protocols, and authorization flows, must be reproduced faithfully, while the underlying computation, model inference and tool ex- ecution, must never occur. We present InferD, a low-interaction honeypot framework organized around a single principle we call deception without inference: every request an adversary can observe is answered from static response pools, and nothing an adversary submits is ever executed. InferD decomposes the emulation into four deception planes, transport, service protocol, vulnerability surface, and agentic session, adds a provenance plane that links a planted credential to evidence of downstream model-mediated processing.
case_studies.summary: InferD is a honeypot framework that lets security teams study how AI inference services are attacked without risking real models or data. It emulates the visible behaviour of LLM APIs, vector stores and orchestration gateways, while all responses come from static pools and no actual inference runs. The result is a low‑interaction trap that provides evidence of attack paths and credential use without exposing real assets.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI inference infrastructure, add InferD to your security stack: 1) deploy the framework on a separate test environment, 2) configure it to mirror your production API endpoints, 3) monitor the static response logs for malicious activity and adjust firewall rules accordingly.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses security of AI inference infrastructure, directly impacting how IT engineers protect public-facing ML services. The framework appears to be a tangible, low-interaction honeypot that could be deployed, indicating moderate maturity. Its applicability as a security service or component of a security-as-a-service offering suggests a clear monetisation path within 90 days.

case_studies.title: The Real Cost of Context: Predicting Compute Time and Energy Consumption in LLM Prefill and Decode Phases
case_studies.abstract: The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) into agentic architectures has substantially increased token consumption, raising concerns about their energy footprint. Yet, estimating the energy consumption of proprietary API-based models remains challenging, and existing approaches focus primarily on generated output tokens while overlooking the impact of the large input contexts characteristic of agentic workflows. To address this gap, we systematically profile compute time and energy consumption across a wide range of prefill (input) and decode (output) token lengths. Using generalized linear models, we show that decode compute time and energy scale linearly with output length, whereas prefill compute time and energy exhibit both linear and quadratic scaling with input length. These findings demonstrate that input context becomes a relevant factor for large-context workloads. Furthermore, we show that compute time serves as a reliable proxy for energy consumption when direct energy measurements are unavailable. Our mapping framework enables precise energy estimation and supports more sustainable deployment decisions for agentic AI.
case_studies.summary: This research shows how the energy used by LLMs grows with both the input (prefill) and output (decode) tokens, giving clear scaling rules and a simple way to estimate energy from compute time. It builds a profiling tool and statistical models that map token lengths to compute time and energy, proving that compute time is a good stand‑in for energy when measurements are hard to get. The result is a practical framework that can help you predict and reduce the energy footprint of your LLM workloads.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, here is what to do: 1) use the authors’ profiling method to benchmark your LLM workloads and capture prefill and decode token counts; 2) apply the linear/quadratic scaling equations to estimate compute time and energy; 3) adjust your deployment (e.g., limit context length or batch size) to stay within energy budgets and improve sustainability.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper offers empirical insights into energy and compute consumption of LLMs, which can inform cost‑management decisions for IT engineers deploying large models. It is a mature study with released profiling data, but it does not provide a ready‑to‑deploy tool or service, so monetisation potential is limited to internal optimization.

case_studies.title: When Relevant Code Is Wrong: Runtime-Aware Context for AI Coding Agents
case_studies.abstract: AI coding agents increasingly rely on retrieved code and development history to guide software changes. However, highly relevant artifacts may describe implementations that are inactive or incompatible with the target deployment. Neither semantic similarity nor recency establishes whether retrieved information remains applicable under feature flags, architectural migrations, and deployment-specific configurations. We challenge relevance-oriented retrieval by introducing operational context validity, a task-, deployment-, and time-dependent criterion for determining whether software evidence can legitimately guide implementation decisions. We instantiate this new retrieval principle in CASE, an agent-agnostic framework that connects repository artifacts with runtime configurations and architectural evolution, classifies evidence as valid, invalid, or unknown, and generates context packages distinguishing actionable guidance from historical rationale and unresolved constraints. We investigate its feasibility through a reproducible preliminary evaluation involving six development tasks, 15 artifacts, and three deployments. Conventional retrieval exposes 16 incompatible artifact occurrences as actionable, whereas CASE excludes them while retaining all applicable artifacts under the prototype's reference rules. Recency filtering reduces valid recall to 0.43, while removing feature-flag evidence from CASE reduces it to 0.13. Although these results demonstrate feasibility rather than improvements in coding-agent correctness, they reveal limitations of relevance-based retrieval and motivate a new research direction: enabling coding agents to reason not only about which information is relevant, but also whether it remains operationally valid.
case_studies.summary: This research tackles the problem of coding agents misusing older code that no longer runs because of feature flags or architectural changes. The authors built CASE, a framework that links repository code to current runtime settings, classifying artifacts as valid or invalid for guidance. The prototype showed it can filter out 16 previously misapplied artifacts while keeping all applicable ones, proving the idea works but not yet improving agent accuracy.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure, check your code‑retrieval tools: 1) Integrate runtime metadata (feature flags, deployment configs) into your search queries; 2) Filter out artifacts flagged as invalid by your context‑aware system; 3) Verify that remaining code matches current environment before use.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper addresses operational context for AI coding agents, which could impact how engineers integrate code retrieval tools with deployment configurations, but it is still a preliminary prototype with limited practical deployment. The maturity is low as it lacks a fully deployed system, and monetisation potential is minimal because it does not present a ready-to-use product or service.

case_studies.title: Elucidating the Design Space of LM Data Attribution
case_studies.abstract: Data attribution methods for Language Models (LMs) are typically evaluated using downstream tasks like fact retrieval. However, existing evaluations vary multiple dataset properties simultaneously, making it impossible to isolate exactly why an attribution algorithm fails. To diagnose these failures, we explore the design space of LLM data attribution, with a primary focus on evaluation. We introduce the Controlled Attribution Benchmark (CATT) for fact tracing, in which we fine-tune LLMs on entirely fictitious knowledge, providing unambiguous ground truth for attribution. This synthetic setup allows us to systematically alter one dataset configuration at a time, such as document redundancy and lexical distractors. With this configurable evaluation, we demonstrate that redundancy and distractors consistently degrade attribution performance. Rather than proposing a new estimator, we examine two design choices that are underexplored: the loss used to compute gradients and how per-token attribution scores are aggregated into a document score. We find that the true causal evidence within a training document is highly localized, but standard methods dilute this evidence into noise by averaging attribution scores across the entire document. We find that replacing standard cross-entropy loss gradients with the negative log-odds gradients surfaces the critical tokens from other uninformative ones. We can then aggregate only the top token scores to improve ground truth recall by 35 to 72 percentage points across multiple baselines on our diagnostic benchmark. The negative log-odds correction also generalizes to FTRACE-TREX, improving counterfactual retraining performance for every method we test, by up to 4.9x.
case_studies.summary: Not relevant to IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a synthetic benchmark and loss‑based tweaks to improve attribution quality in language models. While the techniques could inform downstream tools for debugging or compliance, the work is largely research‑benchmarked, lacks a ready‑to‑deploy system, and offers limited immediate utility for infrastructure engineers or SaaS tooling. The potential to sell or deploy within 90 days is low, as it would require substantial integration effort. Thus overall impact, maturity, and monetisation are modest.

case_studies.title: TextSeal2: Distortion-Free LLM Watermarking with Copula Mixing and Memoryless Races
case_studies.abstract: We present TextSeal2, a distortion-free watermark for large language models that keeps its signal under speculative decoding: tokens that replace rejected drafts remain watermarked with the same keys, and the acceptance rate is unchanged. It also preserves output diversity and adds no measurable inference latency. Its predecessor, TextSeal, restores diversity in the Gumbel-max scheme by routing each token to one of two keys via a coin flip. This is suboptimal because the detector averages the scores from both keys without knowing which key was used. TextSeal2 instead merges two or more keys into a single virtual key and couples it to fresh noise through AutoMark's Gaussian copula. Any number of keys, including publicly shared keys, can be merged this way without diluting detection. Under speculative decoding, TextSeal2 verifies keyed drafts with one more exponential race, run on the leftovers of the draft races. By memorylessness, this race reproduces block verification, so the output follows the target model exactly. We evaluate TextSeal2 on three LLMs. At equal output token diversity, TextSeal2 detects 8 to 22 percentage points more 100-token answers than TextSeal at a false-positive rate of $10^{-3}$, and is comparable to textGrain while requiring no post-logits optimization. Under speculative decoding, it detects 18 and 22 percentage points more 200-token answers than TextSeal and textGrain, respectively, at the same acceptance rate.
case_studies.summary: TextSeal2 is a watermark that lets you recognise AI‑generated text without hurting model speed or quality. It merges multiple keys into one, keeping the signal clear even when the model uses speculative decoding. The result is higher detection rates (8‑22% better) with no extra latency. This is relevant to anyone who needs to prove text authenticity in a cloud‑hosted LLM service.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud‑hosted LLMs, enable TextSeal2 by: 1) merge your existing watermark keys with a Gaussian copula in the model’s post‑processing; 2) adjust your inference pipeline to run the extra exponential race only on draft leftovers; 3) monitor detection metrics to confirm no latency increase.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper proposes a watermarking technique for large language models, which is more relevant to model developers than IT engineers managing infrastructure. The method appears to be a research prototype with limited evidence of deployment. While it could be packaged as a service for SaaS providers, the immediacy of monetisation for typical UK IT engineers is low.
